title: Distance to the Nearest Zero
statement:
You get a grid grid of 0s and 1s with at least one 0. Moving one step means going to the cell directly above, below, left or right.

Return a grid of the same size where each cell holds the fewest steps from that cell to any cell containing 0. Cells that hold 0 get 0.

examples.why: The centre is 2 steps from either corner zero. The top-right corner is 2 steps from both zeros too.
One row: the distance grows by one per step away from the only zero.
Steps are only up, down, left and right. The bottom corners need 3 steps, not the 2 a diagonal move would allow.

hints: Running a BFS from every 1 to find its nearest 0 repeats a lot of work. Can you search from the other side?
Start one BFS from all the 0s at the same time. The first time the search reaches a cell, it arrives from the nearest zero.
Put every 0 in the queue at distance 0 and mark the 1s as unvisited. Each popped cell gives its unvisited neighbours its distance plus one.

explain.intuition:
Asking "how far is the nearest zero?" separately for every cell means one search per cell. Flip the question: let all the zeros spread outwards together, one ring per step, like ripples from several stones dropped at once. A cell gets wet first from the closest zero, so the step at which a ripple first reaches it is its answer.

That is a multi-source BFS: an ordinary BFS whose queue starts with every zero instead of one start cell. Each cell enters the queue once, so the whole grid is solved in O(rows · cols). There is also a two-pass DP: sweep top-left to bottom-right using the up and left neighbours, then bottom-right to top-left using down and right.
steps: Create the answer grid. Set zeros to 0 and put them all in the queue; set every 1 to infinity (unvisited).
Pop a cell. For each of its four neighbours inside the grid with a larger distance than the popped cell's distance + 1, set it to that value and push it.
Repeat until the queue is empty.
pitfalls: Running a separate BFS from each 1. It is correct but O((rows · cols)²) on a grid with few zeros.
Starting BFS from only one zero, which gives distances to that zero instead of the nearest one.
In the DP version, doing only one sweep. A cell whose nearest zero lies below or to the right gets the wrong value.

solutions.title: BFS from every cell
solutions.idea: For each 1, run a BFS until it meets a 0.

solutions.title: Multi-source BFS from all zeros
solutions.idea: Seed the queue with every zero at distance 0 and spread outwards; each cell is settled the first time it is reached.

solutions.title: Two sweeps of DP
solutions.idea: A shortest path to the nearest zero first goes up/left or down/right. Sweep forward taking up and left neighbours, then backward taking down and right.

followups: Diagonal steps are allowed too. What changes in the BFS, and does the two-sweep DP still work?
Some cells are walls that cannot be crossed. Which of the two fast solutions still works?
